findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via innerHTML in Test Runner
findings.description: The test/test_runner.html file uses innerHTML to inject data from mock Chrome messages directly into the DOM without sanitization. The lines `out.innerHTML += ...` concatenate user-controlled data (from content script extraction) into the page. While this is a test file and not shipped to production, if the test runner is used with live data or the pattern is copied, it enables stored XSS through crafted tweet text or author fields.
findings.recommendation: Replace innerHTML usage in the test runner with safe DOM APIs (createElement, textContent) consistent with the production feed.js approach. Even test files should model secure practices.

findings.title: Unbounded Message Processing Without Origin Validation
findings.description: In background.js, the chrome.runtime.onMessage listener accepts LOG_BATCH messages from any content script without verifying the sender's origin or tab URL. While Manifest V3 limits message senders to the extension's own scripts, a compromised or malicious content script injection on the matched host_permissions domains could send arbitrarily large batches to fill storage.
findings.recommendation: Validate sender.tab.url against expected domains (x.com, twitter.com) before processing messages. Also validate message.items is an array and each item conforms to the expected schema.

findings.title: No Input Validation or Sanitization on Stored Data
findings.description: The mergeAndSave function in background.js accepts arbitrary objects from the LOG_BATCH message items array and stores them directly into chrome.storage.local without any schema validation. Malformed or malicious fields (e.g., excessively long text, unexpected field types, prototype pollution payloads via __proto__ keys) are persisted without checks. The feed.js rendering uses textContent (safe), but other consumers of this data could be vulnerable.
findings.recommendation: Implement schema validation for LogItem objects before storage. Validate field types (key: string, type: enum, url: string URL, seenAt: number), enforce maximum string lengths, and reject items with unexpected properties.

findings.title: Image URL Loading Without Domain Allowlist
findings.description: In feed.js, image elements are created with img.src set to the url field from stored data (line 129). While referrerPolicy='no-referrer' is set, there is no validation that the URL points to an expected domain (e.g., pbs.twimg.com). A manipulated storage entry could cause the side panel to load images from arbitrary external servers, enabling tracking pixels or SSRF-like behavior from the user's browser.
findings.recommendation: Validate that image URLs match expected Twitter/X media domains (pbs.twimg.com, video.twimg.com) before setting img.src. Reject or skip items with URLs pointing to unexpected hosts.

findings.title: Link href Set From Untrusted Storage Data Without Validation
findings.description: In feed.js createCard(), link.href is set to item.tweetUrl (line 105) and imgLink.href is set to item.tweetUrl (line 137) from storage data without validating that the URL uses https:// or points to x.com/twitter.com. Malicious storage data could inject javascript: URIs. Although textContent is used (preventing HTML injection), a javascript: URL in the href would execute when clicked.
findings.recommendation: Validate that tweetUrl starts with 'https://x.com/' or 'https://twitter.com/' before using it as an href. Reject or replace with '#' for any URL that does not match the expected pattern.

findings.title: Browsing History Leakage via source.pageUrl
findings.description: The content script captures window.location.href and stores it in the source.pageUrl field of every LogItem. This records exactly which X/Twitter pages the user visited and when. While data stays local, if the storage is ever exported or accessed by another extension, this constitutes a browsing history leak.
findings.recommendation: Document this data collection in a privacy policy. Consider whether source.pageUrl is necessary for core functionality, and if not, remove it or make it opt-in.

findings.title: No Rate Limiting on Batch Processing Queue
findings.description: The background.js processQueue function processes all queued batches sequentially without any rate limiting or maximum queue depth. A rapidly firing content script could queue hundreds of batches, causing excessive storage I/O and potentially impacting browser performance.
findings.recommendation: Add a maximum queue depth (e.g., 50 pending batches) and drop or consolidate excess batches. Consider adding a minimum interval between storage writes.

findings.title: Storage Quota Exhaustion via Unbounded Item Size
findings.description: There is no limit on the size of individual text or author fields in stored LogItems. While the total count is capped at 500, extremely large tweet text fields could fill the chrome.storage.local quota (typically 10MB for extensions), causing silent data loss when subsequent writes fail.
findings.recommendation: Truncate text fields to a reasonable maximum length (e.g., 1000 characters for tweet text, 200 for author) before storage.

findings.title: Content Script Exposes Current Page URL in Extension Messages
findings.description: The content script sends window.location.href as part of every LOG_BATCH item via chrome.runtime.sendMessage. This data traverses the extension's internal messaging channel. While confined to the extension context, it creates an unnecessary data flow of the user's exact browsing location within the X/Twitter domain.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate whether source.pageUrl is needed. If it serves no UI purpose, remove it from the message payload to minimize data exposure.

findings.title: Overly Broad Host Permissions
findings.description: The manifest declares host_permissions for https://x.com/* and https://twitter.com/*, which grants the content script access to all pages on these domains including settings, DMs, and account pages. The extension only needs to observe timeline/tweet pages.
findings.recommendation: Consider narrowing host_permissions to specific URL patterns if possible (e.g., https://x.com/*/status/*, https://x.com/home). However, note that X's SPA routing may make this impractical.

findings.title: No Content Security Policy Defined for Extension Pages
findings.description: The manifest.json does not define a content_security_policy for extension pages (feed.html). While Manifest V3 has strict defaults that block inline scripts and eval, explicitly defining a CSP would provide defense-in-depth and make the security posture clear.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit content_security_policy in manifest.json to restrict script sources and object sources for extension pages.
